rows.en: However, in the Land of Israel too the study of the Torah was at times held back in its course, but this delay did not cause them to draw away from religion and from the Torah. Rather, at all times their longing for it grew stronger in the face of the misfortunes of the time. The heavy war, too, that took place between Antiochus the Great and Ptolemy the Third and the Fourth, kings of Egypt, brought many and grievous troubles upon Israel. But these troubles did not befall them because they were Jews, for Antiochus the Great was not an enemy of the Jews out of hatred of their religion; rather, the evils came in the wake of the war and harmed the Jews as they harmed all the inhabitants of the land of Syria and all the other lands around it over which the war spread its wings. Then too, when Antiochus prevailed and the land of Judah remained under his rule as before, they rested from their hardships and recovered from their troubles, and all the children of Israel now had relief and peace. At that time the head was the high priest Simeon son of Onias the Second, son of Simeon the Just the First. To Simeon the Second, too, the people of his generation gave a title of praise and called him: Simeon the Just. In his days or a little after him lived Joshua ben Sira. This Joshua praises in his book the excellence of Simeon, and calls him great among the Jews and one who sought the good of his people. He tells of him that he founded the holy service and did many good things for Israel by completing the building of the Temple (Ben Sira ch. 50). And he succeeded in doing all this with the help of Antiochus. He gave them permission to complete the building of the House, and commanded his general, who was in Judea at that time, that everything needed for completing the building of the House be given them free, without money. These days of tranquillity were fit for working to strengthen the religion. The great court in Jerusalem, too, was at that time in its full strength. For in the letter that Antiochus wrote to his general, Antiochus praises the Jews who received him with honour when he came to Jerusalem and went out to meet him with all the men of the council at their head. He also wrote that it should be a statute not to be transgressed that the Jews should have the right to conduct all their affairs according to the law of their Torah, and that the men of the great council should be exempt from the poll tax (Josephus, *Antiquities* 12, 3). It follows that at that time the great court was in its full strength. And indeed, if we are told that in the days of Simeon the Just the First the Great Assembly ceased, this was only a temporary cessation. In a short time it returned to its former state, but under another name: for instead of the name Great Assembly its name was changed to be called by the name Sanhedrin. For since this was the highest office in the nation, it is self-evident that they were forced to call it by a name understood by the Greeks, who were the rulers of the land. However, this too is self-evident: that at the time of the great persecution of the Jews in the days of the son of Antiochus the Great, when the government tried to abolish the Torah and the religion as a whole, this office too was abolished for some time.

For the days of tranquillity under the rule of Antiochus the Great did not last long. Antiochus Epiphanes, who reigned after him, was not like his father; from the day he came to the throne until his end he was an enemy of the Jews whose like had not been before him, nor arose after him among all the Seleucid kings of Syria and all the Ptolemaic kings of Egypt. At the beginning of the reign of this oppressor, Antigonus of Sokho stood at the head of the Sanhedrin. True, according to what is related in the Mishnah he received [the tradition] from Simeon the Just, who was one of the last of the Great Assembly, and this Simeon the First lived a long time before the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes. But if we consider the chain of high priests who lived and worked after Simeon the First, we find that in the days after Simeon there was no reason to transfer the headship of the Sanhedrin from the high priest to another man from among the people. For after Simeon's death his brother Eleazar became priest, and after him Manasseh, his younger brother, who held his priesthood only for a short time, for he died, and in his place came Onias, the son of Simeon; and after his death Simeon the Second became priest, who was also given the epithet "the Just." All these high priests were faithful to the Lord and to Israel. And all the historians of the Jews of that time, when they mention the heads of the great court, mention only the high priest, for the high priest was always the first and the head in the great court of every period. And now we see Antigonus, who was not a priest, rise and become head. This is impossible without a compelling cause, and this fact will shed light on the time of Antigonus; we will judge from it that Antigonus was not head after Simeon, nor during all that time from Simeon the First to Simeon the Second. But after the death of Simeon the Second, when Antiochus Epiphanes came to the throne, and not long after the beginning of his reign this oppressor appointed high priests one after another, all of whom rebelled against the Lord and forsook the Torah and tried to support the government's wish to destroy the Jewish religion: at that time we see a great cause that moved them to set Antigonus at the head of the Sanhedrin; or at any rate he was the man who held fast to the Torah of the Lord. And indeed, if we are told in the Mishnah that he received from Simeon the Just, who was one of the last of the Great Assembly, and handed on to Yose ben Yoezer, we will hold from this report two things: one, that he received from Simeon the Just, but not from the first, rather from the second; and the second, that he handed on to Yose ben Yoezer, whose time falls together with that of Antigonus in close succession. But we will not hold that he received from the Simeon who was one of the last of the Great Assembly; and we say that the sameness of the names caused the compiler of the Mishnah to describe Simeon the Second with the title said of Simeon the First.

The personal history of Antigonus is hidden from us, and of his teachings no more than one saying has reached us, namely (Avot 1:3): "Be not like servants who serve the master on condition of receiving a reward, but be like servants who serve the master not on condition of receiving a reward; and let the fear of Heaven be upon you." From the content of this saying one may judge that the days of his headship were evil; and therefore, to strengthen the hearts of the faltering who asked, Where is the reward hoped for by those who do good?, Antigonus taught them that one should not serve the Lord for the sake of the reward, but we should do the good because it is good in itself. And this is not a contradiction of the promises of the Torah (Jost p. 106), which promises good and recompense to those who do good; for Antigonus too never thought that the doing of good is not the cause of reward, but he believed with perfect faith in recompense; only his warning is that our doing of good should not be for this aim alone, and that we should not cease to do good if we see that the hoped-for reward has not reached us, but we should do the good even on condition of not receiving a reward. And it is very likely that the spirit of the opinions of the Greek sages spoke through his tongue when he said that we should not do the good out of hope of receiving a reward; this is exactly the view of the Stoics, who say that there is no merit in doing good and righteousness when they are done for the sake of the pleasure that comes to a person from doing good, or for some other motive, for we do the good because it is good in itself, and in the doing of good is found the reward of good. However, as befell the sages at all times and in all generations, whose words the perverse of heart twisted, whether from folly or from malice, and saw in them thoughts and opinions that the sages had not thought, so it befell Antigonus too. Two of his disciples twisted and corrupted his pleasant words, saying that he meant by his words to teach that there is no judgment and reckoning above; and by this they were caught in the net of heresy and went astray. These disciples were called by name Zadok and Boethus, and from them came the sect of the Sadducees. So the aggadah went and spread (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 5). Whether this is only an exaggerated aggadah or the plain truth, one thing we can hold, and it is that in the days of Antigonus a sect arose that opposed the Pharisees. Which of the events of that time was the cause of its rise has not been preserved for us, and we would seek something certain in vain. Nor should one wonder that a cloud rests upon so great an event as the separation of the Sadducees, which left its mark on all matters of religion and lasted several hundred years. The hardships of the time did this. The evil and the troubles from without grew greater day by day, until a man's tongue grows weary of describing them in words: oppression, plunder and murder spread over the full breadth of the land of Judah "as the waters cover the sea" [Isaiah 11:9]; the religion of the Torah was trampled and those who studied it were persecuted; and in the abyss of such events this event sank, as other events concerning religion and the Torah no doubt sank. It is indeed very possible that at the outset there was no separation of sects, but the basis of the dispute was the rivalry of one man with another. For already from of old the high priesthood had been reserved for the Levitical priests, the sons of Zadok. And it befitted them, for at all times they kept the way of the Lord, and when Israel went astray from the Lord they kept the charge of their office (Ezekiel 44:15 and in many places). And if we consider the chain of high priests from the beginning of the Second Temple to the days of Antiochus Epiphanes, we find that all of them were of the sons of Zadok. But from the days of Antiochus this chain was no longer kept: Onias the Fourth, who was also called Menelaus, was not of the family of Zadok and rose to the high priesthood (see Hitzig, sec. 65)⚠1; and perhaps Yakim too, who is called Alcimus, who was appointed high priest after him, perhaps he too was not of the sons of Zadok; and after that the high priesthood passed to the family of the Hasmoneans, and they too were not of the sons of Zadok. Such a change, overturning an old-established statute and custom, could certainly be a cause of division of opinions and hearts. Therefore it is very possible that from the time the priests of the sons of Zadok were pushed out of the high priesthood, then too a sect began to grow that called itself Sadducees, after the name of the head of their father's house, Zadok.{v1_06_08:1} But all this will not shed light on their character, and we still do not know the cause of the matters of their opposition in the principles of the Jewish religion. For the main point of their opposition is that they opposed the teaching of the elders, which among us is called the Oral Torah; and since they were opposed to this Torah, it is self-evident that their grievance against the teaching of the elders was also the cause of their turning away from following them. And if we say in particular that they denied the resurrection of the dead, this is only because this principle too flows from the teaching of the elders. But this separation was a natural outcome of the change and transformation in opinions and in learning in the course of that time. Even though we know that the way of interpretation of the sages who carried the Oral Torah had not yet widened so much in that early time as in the later time, nonetheless we also know that already in ancient days the Torah began to be interpreted according to the ways of their midrash, which turn away from the plain sense of Scripture; and on the other side, various interpretations of the Torah based on scientific inquiry, in harmony with the wisdom of the Greeks, had already spread at that time. In the days of Ptolemy Philometor, the contemporary of Judah Maccabee, commentaries on the Torah in this manner had already been composed by the Jewish philosopher Aristobulus. And we will see below that the Jews in the Land of Israel too inclined at times to go in this way. And indeed from the conduct of the Alexandrian Jews and their ways it appears that this became a stumbling block for many, until they quickly turned away from keeping the Torah in practice, thinking that the statutes of the Torah are only like hints at intellectual matters, and to these they turned their gaze, but the practice of the statutes was light in their eyes and they were not careful to keep it. Philo the Jew of Alexandria already alluded to these in his book *On Abraham* (p. 401). Now if we consider the character of many of the men of the Torah in our nation, from of old and in all times, we find that division of opinion was mostly born when they saw that a new way in beliefs and opinions caused some light-minded people to turn aside from the Torah. If they found that some of those who sought wisdom went astray through wisdom, then wisdom in general became a sin in their eyes, and they utterly rejected all external wisdom to the very last extreme, and found fault with every new thing that had been revealed to sages who came of late. So it was of old, in general with respect to the sciences and in particular with respect to the interpretations of the Torah. And so it is very possible that the danger that could come to religion through their being drawn after Greek wisdom in understanding the Torah was what caused many not to go even a step beyond the meaning of the words as written in interpreting the Torah; and it is self-evident that whoever holds in this way to the words as written is likewise opposed to the midrash of the sages of the Oral Torah. Now what we are told in the aggadah, that the separation of the Sadducees took place in the time we are dealing with, will be correct. But the thick cloud spread over all matters of the Oral Torah in this period does not allow us to recognize the traces of the separation and the strong force with which the opposition of the Sadducees acted upon the opinions of the Pharisees⚠2; and only after we pass on further along the path of time and consider the course of this Torah and its development up to the end of the period we are dealing with, will a bright light shine for us, to recognize the character of the sects and to know how they acted upon one another.

1.note: ס"ה read as section 65 of Hitzig's history; it may also be a chapter or page.

2.note: Printed הפירושים (interpretations); read as הפרושים, the Pharisees, by context.

rows.en: Indeed, this division of hearts in beliefs and opinions is a sure sign that the study of the Torah was at that time a matter that occupied them. But soon days came when this study was held back. From the day that Antiochus Epiphanes ascended his royal throne, men already began to cry out "violence" against his rule. At the beginning of his reign Israel could still endure the pressure of the oppressor, and their strength to bear it did not fail. For a nation that has learned from its youth to bear a foreign yoke is not easily crushed to the dust so that it cannot rise; but as this oppressor did ever more mightily, the glory of Jacob grew poor in proportion, until this evil rule became a stone of stumbling to the Temple and to the Torah, and a trap and a snare to the inhabitant of Jerusalem [cf. Isaiah 8:14]. The evil scheme he devised against Israel found strong support within the weary nation. The lawless sons of the people lifted themselves up and went whoring after the laws and customs of the Greeks, and their aim was to turn the people of the Lord away from the Torah and to plant the degenerate shoots of a foreign vine [cf. Jeremiah 2:21] on the holy soil. The high priest who stood to serve in the Temple of the Lord when Antiochus came to the throne was called Onias, and he was faithful to God and to his people. His brother was Jeshua [Jason], a man of intrigues and of evil deeds, a traitor to his brother and to the ways of his fathers. This treacherous brother denounced his brother to the king and succeeded in his schemes, and by the power of the bribe he gave the king he became priest in his brother's place. His aim was to plant the laws of the Greeks on the soil of Israel. To reach this aim he contrived to obtain from the king, for the Jews of Antioch, the rights of citizens of the city in Jerusalem⚠1, for they had learned to act as the Greeks and their wanton ways; therefore he hoped through their help to reach his goal in Jerusalem. He also obtained permission from the king to set up and establish houses of games, to train the youths of Israel in the games of the Greeks. With these games he began, but their end was evil and bitter; for not many days passed before they already scorned the holy covenant and covered their nakedness from the reproach of the Greeks, until many forsook this sign of the covenant and did not circumcise their sons. True, this priest did not last long in his priesthood, for three years later he fell from his greatness. But the one who came after him was worse than he. The government removed him and installed by force a man who was not of the seed of the priests fit to be high priests; he was called Onias, and by his Greek name Menelaus. With his help and by his counsel all the abominations were done in Israel, as is told in the books of the Maccabees and in the books of Josephus ben Gorion the priest.{v1_06_09:1} Israel in its myriads fell plundered at the feet of the mad king. He robbed and despoiled the treasury of the House of the Lord, profaned the Temple, took away the daily offering and set the abomination that makes desolate (Daniel 11:31, 32) on the altar of the Lord. Keeping the Torah and the commandment became a capital crime, and "they that are wise among the people, who instruct many," fell by fire and flame, by captivity and by spoil (ibid. 33). But the fall of this false priest too came quickly, and the fruit of his deeds was returned upon him. Yet the one who came after him was no better than he, for he too walked in the ways of the Greeks, and his hand was with the government's decree to cut off religion and Torah; he shed much innocent blood, and many of the sages of the Torah and of the pious of the Most High fell slain on the high places of Israel. Yet with all the upheaval that Antiochus Epiphanes wrought in the land of Judah, his wish did not prosper in his hand to cut off the Torah, nor its study. Who would believe our report when we say that the persecutions with which Antiochus the wicked persecuted Israel did not have the power to weaken faith and the study of the Torah among many of the people? And yet so it was. As from of old pressure and compulsion have never had power to accomplish anything against the character of people of strong qualities, but rather the reverse (for the more their opponents and oppressors compel them and try to turn them by force from their opinion and their faith, the more they too add strength and might to hold fast to their opinion and their faith and to turn back all pressure and compulsion by their strength and the firmness of their spirit), so it was at the time when Antiochus rose up to turn Israel from their religion by compulsion and cruel pressure: strong groups bound themselves together and took courage to reach this goal. On the one hand the government pressed them, through the religious decree, to dissolve⚠2 the Torah and to remove the spirit of the Jewish religion from the land, and it was helped also by the lawless among the Jews, for many of the people, and also of the priests, followed it and tried to carry out its counsels by holding to the laws of the Greeks. The high priest called Yakim, and by his Greek name Alcimus, who rose in place of Menelaus, was the worst of all in strengthening the hands of transgressors, in breaking the Torah and in pursuing in wrath those who held to the religion. He made a great slaughter among the sages and the pious of the Most High, and slew all that were pleasant to the eye [Lamentations 2:4]. But against these groups stood righteous men, pious ones of the living God and sages of the Torah, and they took their stand like an iron pillar at the head of the people and kept the charge of religion, so that root and branch should not be cut off. These scorned their lives unto death on the field of slaughter to sanctify the honoured and awesome Name; and those took their lives in their hands to transgress the cruel decrees of the king and to hold to the Torah. They guarded it as the apple of the eye, and led the people with understanding and knowledge not to turn aside from the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God.

1.he: להשתדל בעד היהודים אשר באנטוכיא את משפט אזרחי העיר בירושלים מאת המלך
1.note: Rendered literally; the sentence is ambiguous. 2 Maccabees 4:9 has Jason enrol the men of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch.

2.note: Printed להמוס (perhaps for להמס, to melt, or a misprint for להרוס, to destroy); rendered 'dissolve'.

rows.en: We have now passed in this chapter through a great chapter of the periods of time. It is great in the number of its days and years, and mighty too because of the many events that took place within it in respect of the political state of the Jews; yet the development of the Oral Torah took only small steps forward in it. And how very wonderful is the sight that in the midst of the din of the war that they now waged under the leadership of the Hasmoneans, to stand up for their lives and their religion, now, in the midst of this upheaval, the chain of this Torah grows longer, and for us too the traces of it grow and multiply, which allow us to recognize its nature, its course and its events more and more.
Yose ben Yoezer of Zeredah, Joseph ben Yoḥanan of Jerusalem.

In those days and at that time, when the rod budded and arrogance blossomed [Ezekiel 7:10], and Yakim the high priest, whom the wicked king had made great, did wickedly and went on backsliding in the way of his heart [Isaiah 57:17], adding sin to sin, then two righteous men stood at the head of the people for the teaching and the testimony [Isaiah 8:20], namely: Yose ben Yoezer of Zeredah and Joseph ben Yoḥanan of Jerusalem. They were the first pair of the pairs mentioned in the books of the Talmuds, whose existence continued for several generations. We have already seen in early times the existence of pairs standing at the head of the people, and therefore this institution was not a new thing that had never been before; but it was renewed after it had ceased for a long time. Jehoshaphat king of Judah had already set a pair at the head of the people: one of that pair was appointed to be head in all matters of the Lord, and the second ruler in all the king's matters (above, ch. 4, in the note). And at the time of their first ascent from the exile, Zerubbabel and Jehozadak the priest were the heads; and after them Ezra, with his companion Nehemiah (Graetz vol. 3, p. 107). Although this chief office was divided between two persons, and by human nature agreement between the opinions of different persons is reached only rarely, nonetheless there was no division of opinion between them in those early days on any matter of religion. Indeed, we are told that only on one matter could they not reach a compromise, and Yose ben Yoezer and Joseph ben Yoḥanan are mentioned as the first to disagree. This matter was: whether one should lay hands on the head of the offering on a festival day, to fulfil the word of the Torah "and he shall lay his hand" [Leviticus 1:4], although the act of laying on hands is an action that they forbade as a shevut, both on the Sabbath and on a festival day; or whether we say that one should not lay hands, and the commandment of laying on hands is set aside before the shevut (Hagigah 2:2, and the Bavli and Yerushalmi there). And we are greatly astonished at the sight, when we see that on all the questions concerning the statutes and laws, even though they were divided in their opinions, they agreed in the end on one opinion, while on so light a question as this they could not reach a compromise! How did they not pay attention to the custom of their forebears? Surely at every festival they offered freewill offerings; why did they not look into the matter to see how this had been done up to their time? Especially as it appears that in matters of the offerings, all the days of the Temple, the sages of the generation did not disagree, neither in their own time nor in a later time; and this because the performance of the offerings was in the hands of the priests, and they knew from generation to generation how to act in their work. Therefore it surely did not happen by chance that they found no settlement for this matter, and it is clear that this was one of the questions urgent for their time. But what made this question urgent for that time? Perhaps its urgency was because another question also depends on this question: whether the laying on of hands is indispensable or not? Had they decided that the laying on of hands is indispensable, those living in distant lands would have had no way to send their offerings to the Temple of the Lord, since they could not lay hands on the offering; and this would easily have been a stumbling block to their goal, whose whole aim was to set as a firm foundation that the Temple in Jerusalem should be a holy bond for all who are called by the name of Israel, near and far. Therefore they left the matter undecided, dependent only on the will of the one who brings the offering, whether to come and lay hands or to send his offering (*Darkhei ha-Mishnah* p. 44). But if this were the main point of their dispute, whether the laying on of hands is indispensable, then why did they hang the dispute on laying on of hands on a festival day? Or perhaps we should say that the source from which the report of this matter came was not properly understood, and that when it says there, "this one says to lay hands and this one says not to lay hands," the intent was never about laying on of hands on a festival day; rather, the one who says not to lay hands means that the laying on of hands in general is not indispensable, and the one who says to lay hands means that it is indispensable. But this sense is refuted by what is described of this dispute in the last pair, Hillel and Shammai, from the dispute of whose disciples on this matter (ibid. Mishnah 3) it is clearly proved that the main dispute was on the matter of laying on of hands on a festival day; and so from this last pair we learn the intent of the dispute of the first pairs. Besides this, it is surely strange that in the end they decided and fixed the matter to lay hands (Beitzah 20a; Yerushalmi Hagigah 2:2); did they at that time no longer need a provision for those living in distant lands? Surely they needed it even more, since the dispersion of the Jews also kept growing greatly, and they needed it especially from the time a great community of Jews came to Rome. In truth, however, this question was urgent for them from another side. That is, because it is the axis on which the teaching of the Scribes as a whole turns; and therefore it was the urgent and fitting question for that time, which is the time of the rise of the Sadducees and of those who challenged the Oral Torah. And in this they found no settlement: if a thing that was set as a statute by the elders happens to conflict in some way with a statute of the Torah, does the statute of the sages have power to set aside the statute of the Torah or not? By the decision of this question the teaching of the elders and its force would surely be decided too. Now the act of laying on hands is not a work of labour, and in the plain sense of the words of the Torah it has no root in any way; only the elders set it as a statute to beware also of shevut, and in their view the act of laying on hands too falls under the category of shevut, and why should it be lesser? And they were in doubt whether to set aside the commandment of laying on hands because of the statute of the sages and the elders, to show the stringency of the words of the Scribes and thereby to subdue the Sadducees, or to say the reverse, that this statute has no power to stand against a statute of the Torah. Now if we consider the matter from this side, we find that it was no small thing on which their opinions were divided; rather, a great principle depends on it, which is the foundation of the whole teaching of the elders.

footnotes.en: Let no one wonder at my deciding that their custom was to write the get in Greek for Greeks; for already from of old they had enacted to write it in the Land of Israel in Aramaic, because that language was the common language of the people. And we find that in the days of the Geonim they wrote bills of divorce in Persian in some places. See *Halakhot Gedolot*, Laws of Gittin, and the responsa *Sha'arei Tzedek*.
See the book *Urschrift* by R. Abraham Geiger, p. 100 ff., and what he cites there, p. 104, in the name of Epiphanius.
See the *History of the Jews* by R. Herzfeld, vol. 2⚠1, and the *History of the Jews and their Sects* by R. Mordecai Jost, vol. 1, and the *History of Israel* by the scholar Hitzig, vol. 2.
